segments.text: Portuguese inherited the same welded Latin teens as its sisters — but it kept fewer of them than anyone. Just five. After quinze (15), it starts over with a completely different, much plainer method.

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 4 columns and 5 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: one with no heading, Portuguese, from Latin, build. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.

The shared -ze is Latin decem ("ten") worn thin — the same ten inside dez (10) and dezembro (the old 10th month, from Chapter 9). The digit sits at the front: dois becomes do-, três becomes tre-, quatro becomes cator-, cinco becomes quin-.
Note catorze — Portuguese kept the c- where Spanish says catorce and French quatorze; three worn-down versions of one Latin quattuordecim.

blocks.title: What you've built: And that's where it stops

segments.text: Quinze is the last fused number. From 16 Portuguese does something none of its sisters do so early — the next lesson.

segments.instruction: the digit inside — "três becomes treze, cinco becomes quinze"

segments.text: Count 11 to 15. (Onze, doze, treze, catorze, quinze.) What is the -ze? (Latin decem, "ten" — as in dez, dezembro.) How many fused teens does Portuguese keep, and is that more or fewer than its sisters? (Five — fewer; French and Italian keep six.) Next: 16, where Portuguese starts building numbers a brand-new way.

lessons.title: dezesseis becomes vinte — built from scratch, with the "and" still showing
lessons.gloss: 16–20 — Portuguese breaks earliest, and rebuilds numbers as "ten AND six"

needs: your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Grammar Lens: Ten AND six until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: At 16, Portuguese stops inheriting and starts building. And it does it more openly than any sister: it glues together the living words for "ten," "and," and the digit — and leaves the and right there in the middle where you can hear it.

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 4 columns and 6 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: one with no heading, Portuguese, build, literally. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.

Every one begins with dez ("ten," Chapter 6) and most keep e ("and") — so dezesseis is transparently a little sentence: ten-and-six. (Dezoito swallows the e before the vowel of oito.) You already know every ingredient; nothing here needs memorising, only assembling.

blocks.title: What you've built: Portuguese breaks earliest

segments.text: All three Romance sisters give up fusing partway through the teens — but Portuguese gives up first:

utterances: language: Portuguese. last fused: quinze (15). goes transparent at: 16 — dezesseis.
language: French. last fused: seize (16). goes transparent at: 17 — dix-sept.
language: Italian. last fused: sedici (16). goes transparent at: 17 — diciassette.

segments.text: One inherited Latin system, three different breaking points — and Portuguese is the boldest rebuilder. (German, by contrast, never breaks at all.)
vinte (20) from vīgintī, the same root as French vingt, Italian venti, and English vigesimal.

segments.text: What does dezesseis literally spell out? ("Ten and six" — dez.

e + seis.) At which number does Portuguese break, and how does that compare with French and Italian? (At 16 — earlier; they break at 17.) Why does dezoito have no e? (It's swallowed before the vowel of oito.) Next chapter: numbers in use.
